title: Price Ticker With Late Corrections
statement:
A feed sends you price records as (timestamp, price) pairs. Records can arrive out of order, and a later record for a timestamp you already have is a correction: it replaces the old price for that timestamp.

  • PriceTicker() starts with no records.
  • update(timestamp, price) stores the price for that timestamp, replacing any earlier value for it.
  • current() returns the price at the largest timestamp seen so far (not the most recent call).
  • maximum() returns the highest price among the current records.
  • minimum() returns the lowest price among the current records.

current, maximum and minimum are only called after at least one update. Tests are a list of operations with their arguments; the first creates the ticker, and the expected output has null for operations that return nothing.

examples.why: The correction at timestamp 1 replaces 40 with 20, so 40 no longer counts for maximum.
Timestamp 2 arrived last but 5 is still the latest time, so current is 10. After 5 is corrected to 50, the lowest price is the 30 at timestamp 2.

constraints: current, maximum and minimum are called only after at least one update
hints: A map from timestamp to price handles corrections and current() easily, if you also remember the largest timestamp. The hard part is maximum and minimum.
A heap gives the max quickly, but a correction leaves the old price inside the heap. Can you delete it later instead of now?
Push every (price, timestamp) pair into a max-heap and a min-heap. When asked, peek at the top; if the map says that timestamp's price is different now, the entry is stale, so pop it and look again.

explain.intuition:
The map timestamp → price is the truth: it absorbs corrections and, together with the largest timestamp seen, answers current(). For the extremes you need a structure that finds the max and min fast, but also forgets corrected prices.

Deleting from the middle of a heap is awkward, so don't. Push every record as (price, timestamp) into both a max-heap and a min-heap. A heap entry is valid only if the map still holds that same price for that timestamp. When maximum() looks at the top and finds a stale entry, it pops it and tries again. Each pushed entry is popped at most once, so the extra work spreads out over all the calls. It works like a frontend cache that is invalidated lazily: you only check freshness when you read.
steps: Keep prices, a map from timestamp to price, and latest, the largest timestamp seen.
update(t, p): set prices[t] = p, raise latest if needed, and push (p, t) onto both heaps.
maximum(): while the top of the max-heap is (p, t) with prices[t] ≠ p, pop it. Return the top price. minimum() does the same on the min-heap.
pitfalls: Returning the price from the most recent update call for current(). It must be the largest timestamp.
Checking only that the entry's timestamp still exists. A corrected timestamp is still in the map, so that test never finds anything stale; compare the stored price with the entry's price.
Popping stale entries from the max-heap but forgetting the min-heap has its own stale entries.

solutions.title: Map and full scan
solutions.idea: Store the map and the latest timestamp. Scan every stored price for maximum and minimum.

solutions.title: Two heaps with lazy deletion
solutions.idea: Push every record into a max-heap and a min-heap. Skip entries whose price no longer matches the map when they reach the top.

followups: Replace the heaps with one sorted structure that counts how many timestamps hold each price. How do corrections update it?
Also answer the average price over all current records in O(1).
